source_text: Quod pertineat, frater, ad tuum problema, habes sententiae nostrae responsionem et exhortationem. Porro qui quaerit, an persecutio fugienda sit, sequentem quaestionem quoque iam prospiciat necesse est, an, si fugienda non est, redimenda certe sit. Ultro igitur et de hoc tibi suggeram, definiens persecutionem, quam constat non esse fugiendam, proinde nec redimendam. Pretium interest; ceterum sicut fuga redemptio gratuita est, ita redemptio nummaria fuga est. Certe et huius timiditatis consilium est. Quod times, redimis, ergo fugis. Pedibus stetisti, curristi nummis. Hoc ipso, quod stetisti, ex redemptione fugisti. Ut autem redimas hominem tu nummis, quem sanguine suo redemit Christus, quam indignum deo et dispositionibus eius, qui filio suo non pepercit pro te, ut fieret maledictum pro nobis, quia maledictus qui pependerit in ligno, qui tamquam ovis ad victimam ductus est et tamquam agnus ante tondentem, sic non aperuit os, sed posuit dorsum suum in flagella, maxillas autem in palmas, et faciem non avertit a sputaminibus, et inter iniquos deputatus est, et traditus est in mortem, mortem autem crucis. Totum hoc, ut nos a peccatis lucraretur. Sol cessit diem emptionis nostrae. Apud inferos remancipatio nostra est et stipulatio nostra in caelis. Sublevatas sunt portae sempiternae, ut introiret rex gloriae, dominus virtutum, hominem de terris, immo ab inferis mercatus in caelos. Quis est nunc, qui adversus illum reluctatur, immo depr(??)tiat mercem eius tam magno comparatam, pretiosissime scilicet sanguine, et commaculat? Iam ergo melius fugere quam fieri viliorem, si non tanto(??)sihi constabit homo, quanti constitit domino. Et dominus quidem illum redemit ab angelis munditenentibus potestatibus, a spiritualibus nequitiae, a tenebris huius aevi, a iudicio aeterne, a morte perpetua. Tu autem pro eo pacisceris cum delatore vel milite vel furunculo aliquo praeside sub tunica et sinu, quod aiunt, ut furtivo, quem ceram toto mundo Christus emit, immo et manumisit. Hunc ergo liberum pretio aestimabis et pretio possidebis, nisi eodem, quanto, ut diximus, domino constitit, sanguine sue scilicet? Ut quid ergo de homine Christum redimis in homine, in quo Christus est? Non aliter et Simon facere temptavit, cum pecuniam apostolis obtulit pro spiritu Christi. Audict ergo et iste, qui se redimens Christi spiritum redemit: Pecunia tua tecum sit in interitum, quoniam gratiam dei pretio consequendam putasti. Quis tamen abnegatorem spernat? Quid enim dicit ille concussor? Da mihi pecuniam. Certe ne eum tradat, siquidem non aliud venditat, quam quod praestaturus est praemio tuo. Cum das, utique ne tradaris voluisti. Non traditus autem traduci habebas? Ergo dum nolendo tradi non vis traduci, nolendo negasti, quod te esse traduci noluisti. Immo, inquis, dum nolo traduci quod sum, sum confessus id esse quod nolo traduci, id est Christianum. Potest itaque te martyrem vindicare constanter ostendisse Christus? Redimens non ostendit. Apud unum, si forte, confessus es, ergo et apud plures nolendo confiteri negasti. Ipsa salus iudicabit hominem excidisse, dum evadit. Excidit ergo qui maluit evasisse. Negatio est etiam martyrii recusatio. Christianus pecunia salvus est, et in hoc nummos habet, ne patiatur, dum adversus deum erit dives. At enim Christus sanguine fuit dives pro illo. Felices itaque pauperes, quia illorum est, inquit, regnum caelorum, qui animam solam in confiscate habent. Si non possumus deo servire et mammonae, possumus et a deo redimi et a mammona? Quis enim magis serviet mammonae quam quem mammonas redemit? Postremo quo exemplo uteris in redemptionem traditionis? Apostoll tractantes persecutionibus agitati quando se pecunia liberaverunt? Quae illis utique non deerat ex praediorum pretiis ad pedes eorum depositis, certe multis locupletibus credentibus viris ac feminis, qui his etiam refrigeria subministrabant. Quando Onesiphorus aut Aquila aut Stephanus hoc modo eis in persecutione succurrerunt? Paulus quidem, cum Felix praeses pecunias accepturum se pro eo a discipulis sperasset, de quo et ipse in secreto tractavit cum ipso, neque ipse pro se neque discipuli pro eo numeraverunt. Illi utique discipuli, qui flentes, quod aeque Hierosolymam tendere perseveraret et persecutiones praedicatas illic non praecaveret, postremo inquiunt: Fiat voluntas dei. Quae ista voluntas? Utique ut pateretur pro nomine domini, non ut redimeretur. Oportet enim, quomodo Christus animam suam posuit pro nobis, ita fieri pro eo et a nobis, nec tantum pro ipso, immo etiam pro fratribus propter ipsum. Quod Ioannes docens non et pro fratribus numerandum, sed moriendum potius pronuntiavit. Nihil interest, si quem Christianum redimere non debeas aut emere. Et adeo voluntas dei sic est. Aspice regnorum et imperiorum utique a deo dispositum statum, in cuius manu cor regis, tanta cotidie aerario augendo prospiciuntur remedia censuum, vectigalium, collationum, stipendiorum, nec umquam usque adhuc ex Christianis tale aliquid prospectum est sub aliqua redemptione capitis et sectae redigendis, cum tantae multitudinis nemini ignotae fructus ingens meti posset. Sanguine empti, sanguine numerati nullum nummum pro capite debemus, quia caput nostrum Christus est. Non decet Christum pecunia constare. Quomodo et martyria fieri possent in gloriam domini, si tribute licentiam sectae compensaremus? Itaque qui eam praemio paciscitur, dispositioni divinae adversatur. Cum igitur nihil nobis Caesar indixerit in hunc modum stipendiariae sectae, sed nec indici umquam tale quid possit, antichristo iam instante et in sanguinem, non in pecunias hiante Christianorum, quomodo mihi proponere potest scripturam esse, Reddite quae sunt Caesaris Caesari? Miles me vel delator vel inimicus concutit, nihil Caesari exigens, immo contra faciens, cum Christianum, legibus humanis reum, mercede dimittit. Alius est denarius quem Caesari debeo, qui ad eum pertinet, de quo tunc agebatur, tributarius, a tributariis scilicet, non a liberis debitus. Aut quomodo reddam quae sunt dei deo, utique proinde imaginem et monetam ipsius inscriptam nomine eius, id est hominem Christianum? Quid autem deo debeo, sicut denarium Caesari, nisi sanguinem quem pro me filius fudit ipsius? Quodsi deo quidem hominem et sanguinem meum debeo, nunc vero in eo sum tempore, ut quod deo debeo expostuler, utique fraudem deo facio id agens, ne quod debeo solvam. Bene observavi praeceptum Caesari reddens quae sunt Caesaris, deo vero quae sunt dei abnegans.
thought_title: Buying one's way out is flight and dishonors Christ's blood
orientation: Tertullian has just concluded that church leaders must not flee in persecution, and now he turns to the related question of whether a Christian may pay money to escape being handed over.
pass_a_gloss: As far as it pertains, brother, to your problem, you have the answer of our opinion and an exhortation. Furthermore, he who asks whether persecution is to be fled must now also look ahead to the following question: whether, if it is not to be fled, it is certainly to be bought off. Therefore I will also of my own accord suggest to you about this, defining that persecution, which it is agreed is not to be fled, likewise is not to be bought off. The price makes the difference; but just as flight is a free buying of one's way out, so a money buying of one's way out is flight. Certainly this is also the counsel of cowardice. What you fear, you buy off, therefore you flee. You stood on your feet, you ran with coins. By this very fact, that you stood, you fled by buying your way out. But that you should buy back a man with coins, whom Christ bought back with his own blood, how unworthy of God and of his arrangements, who did not spare his own Son for you, so that he might become a curse for us, because cursed is he who has hung on a tree, who was led like a sheep to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth, but he set his back to the scourges, and his cheeks to blows, and he did not turn his face away from spittings, and he was counted among the wicked, and he was handed over to death, even the death of the cross. All this, so that he might gain us from sins. The sun withdrew on the day of our purchase. Among the dead is our re-transfer, and our covenant is in the heavens. The eternal gates were lifted up, so that the king of glory might enter, the Lord of hosts, having purchased man from the earth, or rather from the dead, into the heavens. Who is there now who struggles against him, or rather cheapens his merchandise bought at so great a price, most precious indeed, by blood, and defiles it? Therefore it is now better to flee than to become cheaper, if man will not cost himself as much as he cost the Lord. And the Lord indeed bought him back from the angels who hold the world, from the spiritual powers of wickedness, from the darkness of this age, from eternal judgment, from perpetual death. But you bargain for him with an informer or a soldier or some petty governor under the tunic and in the bosom, as they say, as with a thief, whom Christ bought for the whole world, or rather also set free. Will you therefore value this free man at a price and possess him at a price, unless at the same price, as we said, he cost the Lord, that is, by his own blood? Why then do you buy Christ back from a man in the man, in whom Christ is? Not otherwise did Simon also try to do, when he offered money to the apostles for the Spirit of Christ. Therefore let this man also hear, who by buying himself off bought off the Spirit of Christ: Let your money be with you unto destruction, because you thought the grace of God was to be obtained by a price. Who, however, would despise a denier? For what does that extortionist say? Give me money. Certainly so that he may not hand him over, since indeed he sells nothing other than what he is going to perform for your reward. When you give, you certainly wanted not to be handed over. But if you were not handed over, were you going to be exposed? Therefore while by not wanting to be handed over you do not want to be exposed, by not wanting you have denied what you did not want yourself to be exposed as being. But rather, you say, while I do not want to be exposed as what I am, I have confessed that I am what I do not want to be exposed as, that is, a Christian. Can Christ therefore claim you as a martyr for having shown it constantly? He who buys himself off does not show it. Before one man, if perhaps, you have confessed, therefore also before many by not wanting to confess you have denied. Salvation itself will judge that a man has fallen away, while he escapes. Therefore he has fallen away who preferred to have escaped. Denial is also the refusal of martyrdom. A Christian is saved by money, and for this he has coins, so that he may not suffer, while he will be rich against God. But Christ was rich with blood for him. Blessed therefore are the poor, because theirs is, he says, the kingdom of heaven, who have only their soul in their property. If we cannot serve God and money, can we be both bought back by God and by money? For who will serve money more than he whom money has bought back? Finally, by what example do you use buying one's way out of being handed over? The apostles, tossed about by persecutions, when did they free themselves by money? Which money was certainly not lacking to them from the prices of lands placed at their feet, certainly with many wealthy believing men and women, who also supplied refreshments to them. When did Onesiphorus or Aquila or Stephen help them in this way in persecution? Paul indeed, when Felix the governor had hoped that he would receive money for him from the disciples, about which he also dealt with him in private, neither he for himself nor the disciples for him paid. Those disciples indeed, who weeping, because he continued to press on equally to Jerusalem and did not guard against the persecutions foretold there, finally say: Let the will of God be done. What is this will? Certainly that he should suffer for the name of the Lord, not that he should be bought off. For it is necessary, just as Christ laid down his own life for us, so it should be done for him also by us, and not only for him, but rather also for the brothers for his sake. Which John, teaching, declared that it should not be paid even for the brothers, but rather that one should die. It makes no difference, if you ought not to buy back or purchase any Christian. And so the will of God is thus. Look at the state of kingdoms and empires, certainly arranged by God, in whose hand is the heart of the king, so many remedies of taxes, tributes, contributions, and payments are daily provided for increasing the treasury, and never up to now has any such thing been provided from Christians, to be reduced under some buying off of person and sect, although from so great a multitude, known to no one, an immense profit could be reaped. Bought by blood, counted by blood, we owe no coin for our head, because our head is Christ. It is not fitting that Christ should cost money. How could martyrdoms come to be for the glory of the Lord, if we should compensate the license of the sect by tribute? Therefore he who bargains for it by a reward opposes the divine arrangement. Since therefore Caesar has imposed nothing on us in this manner of a tribute-paying sect, but neither could any such thing ever be imposed, since the antichrist is already pressing in and gaping for the blood, not for the money, of Christians, how can he propose to me the scripture, Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's? A soldier or an informer or an enemy shakes me down, exacting nothing for Caesar, but rather acting against him, when he dismisses a Christian, guilty by human laws, for a fee. The denarius which I owe to Caesar is another one, which belongs to him, about which it was then being dealt with, owed by tribute-payers, that is, not by free men. Or how shall I render to God the things that are God's, certainly likewise the image and coin of his inscribed with his name, that is, the Christian man? But what do I owe to God, just as the denarius to Caesar, except the blood which his Son poured out for me? But if I owe to God indeed the man and my blood, now truly I am in that time, that what I owe to God is being demanded, certainly I commit fraud against God by doing this, so that I may not pay what I owe. I have well observed the precept, rendering to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, but denying to God the things that are God's.

choices.english: money buying of one's way out
choices.why: Keeps the glossary term 'buying one's way out' and makes explicit the contrast with free flight; 'nummaria' is rendered as 'money' to preserve the monetary sense.

choices.english: free buying of one's way out
choices.why: Preserves the paradox Tertullian is making: flight is itself a form of buying one's way out, but without cost.
Uses the glossary term for the one who threatens Christians to extract money.
Renders the passive of traduco in the sense of being publicly exposed or brought to trial as a Christian; keeps the distinction from 'tradaris' (handed over).
Uses the glossary term 'money' for mammona, avoiding the archaic 'Mammon'.
Renders the idea of a sect made subject to tribute or taxation, preserving the fiscal metaphor Tertullian is developing.

pass_b_english: As for your question, brother, you now have my answer and my urging. But anyone who asks whether persecution should be fled must also look ahead to the next question: if it should not be fled, should one at least buy one's way out? So I will go further and offer you my view on this too. I hold that persecution, which we have established should not be fled, should likewise not be bought off. The price is the only difference. Just as flight is a free buying of one's way out, so money buying of one's way out is flight. Certainly it is also a counsel of cowardice. You buy off what you fear, therefore you flee. You stood your ground with your feet, but you ran with your money. By the very fact that you stood, you fled through buying your way out. But for you to buy a man with money whom Christ bought with his own blood—how unworthy of God and his purposes! He did not spare his own Son for you, so that he became a curse for us, because cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree (Galatians 3:13). He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he did not open his mouth (Isaiah 53:7); he gave his back to the whips and his cheeks to blows, and did not turn his face away from spitting (Isaiah 50:6); he was numbered among the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12) and handed over to death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8). All this, to gain us from our sins. The sun withdrew from the day of our purchase. Our re-purchase was transacted among the dead, and our contract is in heaven. The eternal gates were lifted up so that the King of glory, the Lord of hosts, might enter (Psalm 24:7), having bought humanity from the earth—no, from the dead—into heaven. Who is there now who struggles against him, or rather cheapens his merchandise, bought at so great a price—the most precious blood—and defiles it? Better to flee than to become cheaper, if a man will not cost himself as much as he cost the Lord. And the Lord indeed bought him back from the angels who hold sway over the world, from spiritual forces of wickedness, from the darkness of this age, from eternal judgment, from perpetual death. But you bargain for him with an informer or a soldier or some petty thief of a governor, under your tunic and in your pocket, as they say, as if by stealth—the man whom Christ bought for the whole world, and indeed set free. Will you put a price on this free man and possess him for a price, unless it is the same price he cost the Lord, as we said—his own blood? Why then do you buy Christ back at the cost of a man, in the man in whom Christ is? Simon tried to do the same thing when he offered the apostles money for the Spirit of Christ. So let this man too, who by buying himself out bought out the Spirit of Christ, hear: May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money (Acts 8:20). Who would despise a denier? What does that extortionist say? Give me money. At least so that he will not hand you over, since he is selling nothing other than what he will provide for your reward. When you give, you certainly wanted not to be handed over. But if you were not handed over, were you going to be handed over? Therefore, by not wanting to be handed over, you did not want to be exposed; by not wanting it, you denied what you did not want to be handed over as. But, you say, by not wanting to be handed over as what I am, I have confessed that I am what I do not want to be handed over as—that is, a Christian. Can Christ then claim you as a martyr for having shown yourself steadfastly? Buying your way out does not show it. You confessed before one person, perhaps; therefore by not wanting to confess before many, you denied. Salvation itself will judge that a man has fallen while he escapes. He has fallen, then, who preferred to have escaped. Refusing martyrdom is also denial. A Christian is saved by money, and he keeps coins for this purpose—so that he will not suffer, as long as he is rich against God. But Christ was rich in blood for him. Blessed are the poor, then, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5:3)—those who have only their soul in their possession. If we cannot serve God and money (Matthew 6:24), can we be bought back both by God and by money? For who will serve money more than the man whom money has bought back? Finally, what example do you use for buying your way out of betrayal? When the apostles were driven about by persecutions, when did they free themselves with money? They certainly did not lack it, since the prices of lands were laid at their feet, and there were many wealthy believing men and women who supplied them with refreshment. When did Onesiphorus or Aquila or Stephen help them in persecution in this way? As for Paul, when Felix the governor hoped to receive money from the disciples for him—and he discussed this privately with Paul himself—neither Paul for himself nor the disciples for him paid anything. Those disciples, weeping because he still insisted on going to Jerusalem and did not avoid the persecutions foretold there, finally said: Let the will of God be done (Acts 21:14). What was that will? Surely that he should suffer for the name of the Lord, not that he should be bought off. For just as Christ laid down his life for us, so it must be done for him by us—and not only for him, but even for the brothers for his sake. John taught this when he declared that we should not buy back the brothers, but rather die for them (1 John 3:16). It makes no difference whether you should not buy a Christian or should not purchase one. And so the will of God is this. Look at the state of kingdoms and empires, surely arranged by God, in whose hand is the heart of the king. Every day so many remedies are devised for increasing the treasury—censuses, taxes, contributions, tributes—and never up to now has anything of this kind been devised against Christians, to reduce them under some buying one's way out for their lives and their sect, although from so great a multitude, known to everyone, an enormous profit could be reaped. Bought with blood, paid for with blood, we owe no coin for our head, because our head is Christ. It is not fitting for Christ to cost money. How could martyrdoms happen for the glory of the Lord if we compensated for the sect's license with a payment? Therefore the man who bargains for it with a price opposes the divine purpose. Since Caesar has imposed nothing on us in the way of a tribute-paying sect—nor could he ever impose such a thing, with the antichrist already pressing in and gaping for the blood, not the money, of Christians—how can anyone propose to me the Scripture, Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's (Matthew 22:21)? A soldier or an informer or an enemy shakes me down, demanding nothing for Caesar—indeed acting against Caesar—when he lets a Christian, guilty under human laws, go for a fee. The denarius I owe Caesar is another matter, one that belongs to him, the tribute that was then under discussion—owed by tribute-payers, not by free men. Or how shall I render to God the things that are God's—that is, his image and coinage inscribed with his name, the Christian man? What do I owe God, as I owe Caesar a denarius, except the blood that his Son poured out for me? But if I owe God my humanity and my blood, and I am now in the time when what I owe God is being demanded, then surely I defraud God by acting to avoid paying what I owe. I have kept the command well—rendering to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, but denying to God the things that are God's.
notes: The source contains two damaged passages: 'depr(??)tiat' (likely 'depretiat', cheapens) and 'tanto(??)sihi' (likely 'tanto sibi', so much for himself). The gloss renders these as 'cheapens' and 'for himself' based on context, but the damage is noted here.

problems.quote: Look at the state of kingdoms and empires, surely arranged by God, in whose hand is the heart of the king (Proverbs 21:1).
problems.source_quote: Aspice regnorum et imperiorum utique a deo dispositum statum, in cuius manu cor regis, ...
problems.why: The source does not cite Proverbs 21:1; the English adds a scripture reference not present in the Latin.
problems.fix: Remove the parenthetical citation or replace with no citation: "Look at the state of kingdoms and empires, surely arranged by God, in whose hand is the heart of the king."

problems.quote: Certainly he says it so that he will not hand you over
problems.why: Source means 'at least so that he does not hand him over'; 'he says it' adds a verb not in source and misreads the construction.
problems.fix: At least so that he will not hand you over,
problems.ruling: Adds ‘he says it’, not in ‘Certe ne eum tradat’ which simply warns ‘lest he hand him over’

problems.quote: were you going to be exposed?
problems.why: traduci means 'to be handed over (to authorities)', not 'exposed'; the same root as tradere throughout this passage.
problems.fix: were you going to be handed over?

problems.quote: by not wanting it, you denied that you were what you did not want to be exposed as
problems.source_quote: nolendo negasti, quod te esse traduci noluisti
problems.why: Source says 'by not wanting, you denied what you did not want to be handed over as'; 'exposed' mistranslates traduci.
problems.fix: by not wanting it, you denied what you did not want to be handed over as.

problems.quote: by not wanting to be exposed as what I am
problems.why: traduci = 'be handed over', not 'exposed'; the extortionist threatens to hand the Christian to authorities.
problems.fix: by not wanting to be handed over as what I am,

problems.quote: I have confessed that I am what I do not want to be exposed as
problems.source_quote: sum confessus id esse quod nolo traduci
problems.why: traduci = 'be handed over', not 'exposed'; consistent mistranslation of the same root.
problems.fix: I have confessed that I am what I do not want to be handed over as

problems.quote: Why then do you buy Christ back from a man, in the man in whom Christ is?
problems.source_quote: Ut quid ergo de homine Christum redimis in homine, in quo Christus est?
problems.why: de homine means 'at the cost of a man' or 'by means of a man', not 'from a man'; the sense is buying Christ at the price of a human being.
problems.fix: Why then do you buy Christ back at the cost of a man, in the man in whom Christ is?
problems.ruling: ‘de homine’ = ‘by means of a man’, not ‘from a man’

problems.quote: who by buying himself off has bought off the Spirit of Christ
problems.source_quote: qui se redimens Christi spiritum redemit
problems.why: Source says 'who by redeeming himself redeemed the Spirit of Christ'—the same act, not 'bought off' twice; 'bought off' trivializes.
problems.fix: who by buying himself out bought out the Spirit of Christ:

problems.quote: to reduce them under some payment for their lives and their sect
problems.source_quote: sub aliqua redemptione capitis et sectae redigendis
problems.why: redemptione = 'buying one's way out' per glossary; 'payment' loses the specific sense of paying to escape persecution.
problems.fix: to reduce them under some buying one's way out for their lives and their sect,

problems.quote: if we paid a tribute to buy license for our sect
problems.why: tribute is not in source; the verb is compensaremus 'compensate/counterbalance', and 'tribute' adds a concept not present here.
problems.fix: if we compensated for the sect's license with a payment
problems.ruling: ‘compensaremus’ ≠ ‘paid a tribute’; added concept absent in source

Changed 'exposed' to 'handed over' in the confession clause; source 'traduci' means 'handed over'.
Changed 'from a man' to 'at the cost of a man'; source 'de homine' means 'at the cost of a man', not 'from a man'.
Changed 'bought off' to 'bought out' for the Spirit of Christ; source 'redemit' means 'redeemed/bought out', and the repetition of 'bought off' trivialized the sense.

problems.quote: John taught this when he declared that we should not pay for the brothers, but rather die for them (1 John 3:16)
problems.why: 1 John 3:16 says 'lay down our lives for the brothers'; 'pay for' is misleading—sounds like paying money.
problems.fix: Render as 'not buy back the brothers' or 'not purchase the brothers.'

variants.text: we should not pay for the brothers

problems.quote: May your money perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with a price (Acts 8:20)
problems.why: Acts 8:20 says 'May your silver perish with you'; 'money' is a loose rendering but not wrong. However 'price' should be 'money' or 'silver' per the Greek.
problems.fix: Align with standard: 'May your silver perish with you, because you thought to obtain the gift of God with money.'

variants.text: May your money perish with you

problems.quote: the eternal gates were lifted up so that the King of glory, the Lord of hosts, might enter (Psalm 24:7)
problems.why: Psalm 24:7 says 'Lift up your heads, O gates'; 'eternal gates were lifted up' is a paraphrase, not a direct quote.
problems.fix: Note the paraphrase or align with standard wording.

problems.quote: he was numbered among the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12)
problems.why: Isaiah 53:12 says 'was numbered with the transgressors'; 'among' vs 'with' is minor but the citation is correct.
problems.fix: No fix needed; this is acceptable.

problems.quote: he gave his back to the whips and his cheeks to blows, and did not turn his face away from spitting (Isaiah 50:6)
problems.why: Isaiah 50:6 says 'I gave my back to those who strike me, and my cheeks to those who pluck out the beard'; 'blows' and 'spitting' are partial.
problems.fix: Note the abbreviated paraphrase or use fuller text.

problems.quote: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's (Matthew 22:21)
problems.why: Matthew 22:21 says 'Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's'; the quote omits 'Therefore' but is otherwise fine.

edits.old: John taught this when he declared that we should not pay for the brothers, but rather die for them (1 John 3:16).
edits.new: John taught this when he declared that we should not buy back the brothers, but rather die for them (1 John 3:16).

edits.old: May your money perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with a price (Acts 8:20).
edits.new: May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money (Acts 8:20).

fixed: Changed 'pay for the brothers' to 'buy back the brothers' to avoid the misleading implication of paying money; the source 'redimendum' means buying back, and 1 John 3:16 is about laying down lives, not paying.
Aligned Acts 8:20 with the standard wording: 'silver' instead of 'money' and 'with money' instead of 'with a price', matching the Greek and the source's 'pecunia'.

Psalm 24:7 paraphrase is acceptable; the English already renders the source's 'sublevatae sunt portae sempiternae' as 'the eternal gates were lifted up', which is a faithful translation of the Latin, not a direct biblical quote.
Isaiah 53:12 'among the transgressors' is acceptable; the source 'inter iniquos' supports 'among', and the citation is correct.

Isaiah 50:6 is an abbreviated paraphrase of the source's 'posuit dorsum suum in flagella, maxillas autem in palmas, et faciem non avertit a sputaminibus', which the English renders accurately; no fix needed.
Matthew 22:21 omission of 'Therefore' is acceptable; the English renders the source's 'Reddite quae sunt Caesaris Caesari' faithfully.

last_rejected.why: 'abnegatorem' = one who denies Christ, not a 'denier' (coin), creating confusion.
last_rejected.fix: Who would despise one who denies Christ?
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'abnegatorem' = one who denies (e.g., Christ); English 'denier' conveys same sense, not a coin term

last_rejected.quote: cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree (Galatians 3:13)
last_rejected.why: The Latin quote comes from Deuteronomy 21:23, not Galatians 3:13.
last_rejected.fix: cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree (Deuteronomy 21:23)
last_rejected.ruling: Tertullian's 'maledictus qui pependerit in ligno' matches Galatians 3:13's citation of Deut. 21:23; referencing Galatians is defensible.
